paragraphs: One-line judgment: Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics are not "parts swappers" but a technical position that diagnoses, adjusts, repairs, or overhauls motor vehicles: checking key components such as belts, hoses, steering, spark plugs, brakes, and the fuel system against a checklist; testing and adjusting repaired systems to manufacturer performance specifications; performing everyday and scheduled maintenance such as oil changes, lubrication, and tune-ups; troubleshooting fuel, ignition, and emissions control system faults with electronic test equipment; and disassembling and inspecting components for wear before repairing or replacing assemblies; people who only want to swap parts by feel and are unwilling to take responsibility for diagnostic conclusions and repair quality are not suited to it.

Signals to keep exploring: you can read service manuals and circuit diagrams and work hands-on per procedure, are willing to test and adjust to manufacturer specifications and record measured values and the basis for judgments honestly, can stop and verify when the symptoms and the diagnosed cause do not match or when high-voltage, airbag, and refrigerant systems are involved, and are willing to communicate symptoms and the repair plan and costs with customers.

Conditions for pausing your investment: you have not yet completed one full vehicle intake—diagnosis—repair—test—delivery loop under any supervised conditions, or you can only describe your interest as "liking cars"; also do not treat being able to drive or being able to take parts apart as proof that you can independently diagnose and repair high-voltage systems, airbag systems, air conditioning refrigerant, or safety parts. Work involving vehicle safety, emissions, new energy high voltage, and refrigerant handling must be carried out per the applicable standards and institutional processes and must leave a traceable basis; this page does not provide diagnosis, repair, or field work instructions.

Education and authorization must be verified separately: O*NET lists 49-3023.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0), and among the education levels published on the page 32% is requiring a postsecondary certificate, 30% is requiring less than a high school diploma, and 26% is requiring a high school diploma or equivalent; the occupation requires prior related work skills, knowledge, or experience, and training is usually one to two years and may include recognized apprenticeship programs. On the U.S. side, air conditioning system repair must be performed for compensation by personnel trained and certified through an EPA-approved program (Clean Air Act Section 609), and there are also ASE certification series (including A1–A9, L1–L4, and ADAS and electric vehicle related certifications). On the mainland China side, motor vehicle repair operations are subject to filing management, and repair parts must have a traceable source and counterfeit or substandard parts must not be used. Education, industry certification, institutional authorization to work and work authorization, and the special operations certificate are different statuses and must be verified item by item according to employer, position, and location.

One line: this is a technical position centered on diagnosis and repair quality and safety procedures; the core is vehicle intake and fault confirmation, inspection and measurement, disassembly and repair and overhaul, testing and adjustment to specification, and work orders and records, rather than an interest in cars or experience with driving.

The work of Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics falls into three categories: diagnosis and inspection (checking key components such as belts, hoses, the steering system, spark plugs, the brake and fuel systems, and wheel bearings against a checklist; inspecting vehicle damage and recording findings; reviewing work orders and discussing them with the supervisor; using electronic test equipment to troubleshoot fuel, ignition, and emissions control system faults; developing work procedures using charts and technical manuals and experience; disassembling units and checking components for wear with micrometers, calipers, and gauges; road-testing vehicles and testing components and systems with infrared engine analyzers, compression gauges, and computerized diagnostic equipment; testing automotive electronic computer components; and diagnosing engine management system or related sensor faults on flexible fuel vehicles); repair and overhaul (performing everyday and scheduled maintenance such as oil changes, lubrication, and tune-ups; repairing and replacing linings and replacing and adjusting brakes; repairing, replacing, or adjusting fuel injectors, carburetor components, and gasoline filters; repairing and maintaining air conditioning, heating, engine cooling, and electrical systems; overhauling or replacing carburetors, blowers, generators, distributors, starters, and pumps; tuning engines; repairing or replacing components such as pistons, connecting rods, gears, valves, and bearings; disassembling, repairing, and rebuilding faulty assemblies such as power and steering systems; repairing or rebuilding transmissions; rebuilding crankshafts and cylinder blocks; replacing spark plugs, fuel filters, air filters, and batteries on hybrid electric vehicles; rewiring ignition systems, lights, and instrument panels; and installing and adjusting or repairing hydraulic or electromagnetic window, seat, and roof lift mechanisms); and delivery and customer communication (communicating with customers to obtain problem descriptions and discuss pending work and future repair needs; estimating repair costs; testing and adjusting repaired systems to meet manufacturer performance specifications; and keeping the work area clean). All three categories presuppose stopping and verifying when the symptoms and the cause do not match or when high voltage, airbags, refrigerant, or safety parts are involved.

The U.S. O*NET49-3023.00 definition is to diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul automotive vehicles; the BLS OOH focuses on automobiles and light trucks. The O*NET details list 30 tasks (25 Core, 5 Supplemental) and 41 work activities and publish Importance: checklist and post-repair testing 87 each, routine maintenance 86; driving or operating vehicles and equipment 82, mechanical maintenance 79, decision making and problem solving and general physical activity 78 each, getting information 75, computer use 65, and recording 58. The scores are occupational group importance, not occurrence frequency or an individual threshold.

entries: Vehicle intake and confirmation | Make the object and requirements clear | Obtain the customer's description of the symptoms and verify vehicle damage and pre-existing problems, review the work order and discuss it with the supervisor, and write out the repair scope and costs and the items to be confirmed.

Diagnosis and inspection | Give the judgment a basis | Check key components against the checklist, measure with diagnostic equipment and gauges, determine the fault scope against manufacturer specifications, and record the measured values and the basis for judgments.

Repair and overhaul | Keep the work reliable | Disassemble and assemble per procedure and protect surrounding components, inspect for wear before repairing or replacing components, assemble and fill to specification, and avoid substituting parts replacement for diagnosis.

Testing and adjustment | Make the result reviewable | Test and adjust repaired systems to manufacturer performance specifications, describe anomalies and deviations, and add diagnosis and review when necessary.

Delivery and records | Make the process traceable | Record the symptoms and inspection and measurements and replaced parts and test results, and explain to the customer what has been handled and what remains pending, along with the costs.

Collaboration and authorization | Make responsibility attributable | Coordinate with the front desk and supervisors and parts management; when safety parts, emissions, high-voltage systems, airbags, and refrigerant handling are involved, follow the authorized process and report open items honestly.

Work environment | 86% wear routine protective or safety equipment every day, 83% are inside enclosed vehicles or operating enclosed equipment every day, 83% handle, control, or feel objects and tools continuously or almost continuously with their hands, 76% need face-to-face discussions every day, 69% are exposed to contaminants every day, 68% work indoors in a controlled environment every day, 59% work indoors without a controlled environment every day, 52% face time pressure every day, 51% are exposed to distracting or uncomfortable noise every day, 41% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day, 39% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, 38% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day, 35% are exposed to extreme heat or cold every day, and 30% are never exposed outdoors to various weather.
Main equipment and tools | Lifts and support equipment, hand and power tools and grinders, micrometers and calipers and gauges, diagnostic scanners and infrared engine analyzers and compression gauges, air conditioning refrigerant recovery and charging equipment, and personal protection (safety glasses, gloves, hearing protection, safety shoes, respiratory protection).
Task rhythm | 52% work more than 40 hours per week; 49% perform repetitive motions continuously or almost continuously, 43% stand continuously or almost continuously, 40% bend or twist continuously or almost continuously, 35% kneel, squat, bend, or crawl more than half the time, 35% walk or run more than half the time, and 36% are in confined work spaces or awkward positions at least once a week.
Collaboration | Work with vehicle owners and front desk reception, workshop supervisors, and parts and inventory management personnel; 44% spend most of their time in contact with others, 38% consider cooperation with the work group or team extremely important, and 27% consider coordinating or leading others extremely important.
Competition and pressure | 36% consider the consequences of errors extremely serious, 46% consider their decisions very important to colleague or company results, 42% have a lot of decision freedom, 36% have some freedom over tasks and priorities and goals, and 56% need to make decisions every day.
Compliance and safety | Shop work must meet the applicable safety and environmental requirements; air conditioning system repair must be performed for compensation by personnel trained and certified through an EPA-approved program (Clean Air Act Section 609); on the mainland China side, motor vehicle repair operations are subject to filing management, and parts must have a traceable source (see the Provisions on the Administration of Motor Vehicle Repair).
Records and review | Symptoms and inspection and measurements and judgments and replaced parts and test results need to be traceable; 46% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, and 26% consider repeating the same task extremely important.
Skills and training | O*NET lists this occupation as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); the basic skills are mainly critical thinking, active listening, monitoring, active learning, and speaking; the cross-functional skills include repairing, troubleshooting, equipment maintenance, operation monitoring, complex problem solving, installation, operation and control, quality control analysis, equipment selection, judgment and decision making, systems analysis, systems evaluation, and time management; knowledge is mainly mechanical, engineering and technology, computers and electronics, customer and personal service, English language, and mathematics; abilities include deductive reasoning, near vision, problem sensitivity, finger and manual dexterity, control precision, inductive reasoning, arm-hand steadiness, information ordering, visualization, and multi-limb coordination (the details publish Importance, not frequency).
Entry and authorization | Education does not equal work authorization, and industry certification does not mean you can handle high-voltage systems and airbags and safety parts in any setting; work must follow institutional processes and the applicable standards.
Industry and employers | The O*NET industry distribution is retail trade 43%, other services 31%, and other industries 26%; common employers are brand-authorized service centers, general auto repair shops, chain quick-repair shops, accident vehicle repair centers, and new energy specialty shops.
Supplementary boundaries | The O*NET new-hire education requirement survey is 32% postsecondary certificate, 30% below high school, and 26% high school or equivalent, which is not the incumbent composition. Zone3/SVP6.0 to <7.0 is an occupational preparation description, usually one to two years of training, not a fixed threshold for every position. The BLS EP typical entry is a postsecondary nondegree award, related experience None, and short-term on-the-job training; the OOH notes that those who have taken related courses may need shorter training, that untrained workers start as assistants or in maintenance positions with longer mentoring, and that a paid apprenticeship pathway is also available; the definitions cannot substitute for one another. U.S. ASE A1–A9 professional certification requires passing the corresponding examination and meeting 2 years of full-time equivalent related hands-on experience; qualifying education can substitute for part of the experience, and the substitutions cannot be combined. The examination can be taken first, and if the experience requirement is not met only the score is held without certification. L1–L4 is 3 years and G1 is 1 year; automotive Master requires A1–A8 all to be certified, A9 is not required, and the relevant certifications are maintained every 5 years. This is not a uniform practical examination or a whole-vehicle work permit. In the United States, for compensation (including barter of services) repair of motor vehicle air conditioning (MVAC), any refrigerant requires Section609 approved training and certification and the use of approved recovery equipment as required; before reuse it must be reconditioned or recycled and purified. The intentional venting prohibition has a SNAP-approved CO2/R744 exception, but that exception does not cancel the Section 609 personnel certification. It applies only to the corresponding U.S. MVAC scenario, not to a general Chinese auto repair certificate or a permit for all air conditioning systems. The OSHA industry hazard PDF contains 2011—2016 NAICS8111 data, with 108 deaths and about 22,200 nonfatal injuries and illnesses in 2016, covering the automotive repair and maintenance industry, which is not the current incidence rate for this occupation; it lists commonly cited 1910.132/133 and other provisions but not 1910.138, so it cannot be used to claim that all PPE regulations or per-model stop and recovery steps have been obtained.

Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics focus on the diagnosis, repair, and overhaul of motor vehicles, covering mechanical and electrical and electronic systems, and are responsible for diagnostic conclusions and repair quality; automotive body and glass repairers focus on sheet metal and painting and also handle glass; automotive glass installers and repairers focus on windshield and window glass disassembly and repair; bus and truck mechanics and diesel engine specialists focus on commercial vehicles and diesel power; motorcycle mechanics focus on motorcycles; automotive engineering technicians focus on test preparation and execution and data collection and usually do not carry responsibility for signing off on repairs; automotive engineers focus on vehicle and system design and development; electric motor and power tool repairers focus on motors and power tools. Adjacent occupations share tool use and safety knowledge, but the objects, deliverables, and responsibilities differ.
Diagnosable, repairable, reviewable repair results

Complete diagnosis and repair per procedure, and leave a work order stating the fault symptoms and the customer's description, the inspection and measurement results, the basis for judgments, replaced parts and quantities, the test and adjustment results, and the parts that remain uncertain, so that the supervisor or quality inspection personnel can judge from it.
Work orders and repair and inspection records

The objects are the mechanical and electrical and electronic systems of motor vehicles (engines, transmissions and drivetrains, brakes, steering and suspension, air conditioning and heating and cooling, fuel and ignition and emissions control, and window, seat, and roof lift mechanisms); the basis is manufacturer service manuals and specifications, the applicable standards and regulations (emissions and safety and refrigerant handling), and the institution's onboarding and quality inspection processes.

Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics (U.S. side O*NET 49-3023.00, Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics) diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul automotive vehicles. The original official duties read "Diagnose, adjust, repair, or overhaul automotive vehicles."; O*NET lists 30 official tasks, focused on checking key components such as belts and hoses and steering and spark plugs and the brake and fuel systems and wheel bearings against a checklist; testing and adjusting repaired systems to meet manufacturer performance specifications; performing everyday and scheduled maintenance such as oil changes, lubrication, and tune-ups; inspecting vehicle damage and recording findings; performing wheel, frame, and steering alignment with specialized equipment; repairing, replacing, and adjusting brakes and fuel injectors and filters; repairing and maintaining air conditioning and heating and cooling and electrical systems; using electronic test equipment to troubleshoot fuel and ignition and emissions control system faults; road-testing and using infrared engine analyzers and compression gauges and computerized diagnostic equipment to test components and systems; communicating symptoms and repair needs with customers; overhauling or replacing carburetors and blowers and generators and distributors and starters and pumps; tuning engines; repairing or replacing pistons and connecting rods and gears and valves and bearings; diagnosing and repairing the engine management systems of flexible fuel vehicles; disassembling, repairing, and rebuilding assemblies such as power and steering systems; disassembling units and checking for wear with micrometers and calipers and gauges; replacing spark plugs and filters and batteries on hybrid vehicles; rewiring ignition and lights and instrument panels; installing and adjusting window, seat, and roof lift mechanisms; estimating repair costs; visually inspecting compressed natural gas systems; repairing or rebuilding transmissions; rebuilding crankshafts and cylinder blocks; and modifying fuel systems with aftermarket products. In the United States this occupation is in Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); mainland China statistics are aggregated by industry category and job category and do not list this occupation separately, and the related work falls under motor vehicle repair business items. This page does not constitute diagnosis, repair, or field work instructions, and the relevant decisions must be made by organizations and personnel with the appropriate qualifications and authorization following the applicable standards and processes.

The individual and the workshop supervisor (or quality inspection personnel)

Diagnostic conclusions, repair quality, and test and adjustment results are the individual's responsibility; matters involving vehicle safety parts, emissions compliance, new energy high-voltage systems, airbags, and refrigerant handling are decided by personnel with the appropriate qualifications and authorization following the applicable standards and processes, and when the basis is unclear or the work is beyond the authorized scope, work must stop and be escalated.
Education and preparation

O*NET lists 49-3023.00 as Job Zone Three (SVP 6.0 to <7.0); most occupations in this zone require vocational school training, related on-the-job experience, or an associate's degree, and require prior related work skills, knowledge, or experience, with training usually one to two years and possibly including recognized apprenticeship programs; among the education levels published on the page, 32% is requiring a postsecondary certificate, 30% is requiring less than a high school diploma, and 26% is requiring a high school diploma or equivalent. O*NET also lists 18 registered apprenticeship titles (such as Automotive Mechanic, Transmission Mechanic, Front-End Mechanic, and Brake Repairer) and 960 training programs (mostly in automotive mechanical technology and automotive engineering technology). On the mainland China side, training is mainly through motor vehicle repair related vocational skills training and mentoring by experienced workers, with specific requirements set by the employer.
Not interchangeable

Education, industry certification (such as U.S. ASE A1–A9 and L1–L4 and ADAS and electric vehicle related certifications), air conditioning repair certification through an EPA-approved program, registered apprenticeship experience, institutional authorization to work and work authorization, and the special operations certificate are different statuses: education does not bring work authorization, and certification does not mean you can independently handle high-voltage systems, airbag systems, or safety parts, or carry out repair work in any setting.

Check at least six items before starting: the occupational definition and the employer entity (O*NET 49-3023.00 is a U.S. definition; on the mainland China side the position and the employer must be identified); education and professional training; the employer's internal authorization to work and the scope of work authorization; the work procedures for diagnosis and repair and testing; the qualification requirements for air conditioning refrigerant and new energy high voltage and airbag-related work; and the pay method (monthly salary, hourly plus commission, or piece rate).
Occupational definition

The U.S. side is O*NET 49-3023.00 (Automotive Service Technicians and Mechanics); on the mainland China side you must first identify whether the position belongs to a brand-authorized service center, a general auto repair shop, a chain quick-repair shop, an accident vehicle repair center, or a new energy specialty shop, because different employers differ greatly in diagnostic equipment, work procedures, and authorization requirements.
Education and major pathways

On the U.S. side a postsecondary certificate and a high school diploma predominate (among the education levels published on the O*NET page, 32% is requiring a postsecondary certificate and 26% is requiring a high school diploma or equivalent, with a further 30% requiring less than a high school diploma), most positions require prior related work skills and one to two years of training, and 18 registered apprenticeship titles exist; on the mainland China side, training is mainly through motor vehicle repair related vocational skills training and mentoring by experienced workers, with specific education requirements set by the employer.
Authorization to work and work permits

Diagnosis, repair, and testing must follow institutional processes and the applicable standards. On the U.S. side air conditioning system repair must be performed for compensation by personnel trained and certified through an EPA-approved program (Clean Air Act Section 609); the O*NET certification page also lists a large number of industry certifications (such as ASE A1–A9, L1–L4, ADAS and electric vehicle related certifications, and per-vehicle-model certifications). On the mainland China side motor vehicle repair operations are subject to filing management, and repair parts must have a traceable source and counterfeit or substandard parts must not be used (Ministry of Transport, Provisions on the Administration of Motor Vehicle Repair, fifth amendment by Order No. 14 of 2023). Before starting, verify pre-job training and work authorization and the quality inspection process; this cannot be inferred directly from education or certification.
Equipment and site safety

Shop work must meet the applicable safety requirements (lifting and support and under-vehicle work protection, hand and power tool and grinder protection, ventilation and personal protection for chemicals and refrigerants and exhaust, mechanical and electrical hazardous energy control, and waste disposal). The O*NET work context shows that 86% wear routine protective or safety equipment every day, 83% are inside enclosed vehicles or operating enclosed equipment every day, 83% handle objects and tools with their hands continuously, 69% are exposed to contaminants every day, 52% face time pressure every day, 41% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day, 39% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, and 38% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day; OSHA industry hazard materials list the industry's common injury events (overexertion in lifting, being struck by objects, slips, trips, and falls, and contact with harmful substances) and the commonly cited penalty provisions (hazard communication 1910.1200, eye and face and hand protection 1910.132/1910.133/1910.138, respiratory protection 1910.134, first aid and eyewash facilities 1910.151, machine guarding 1910.212/1910.215, and electrical 1910.303/1910.305). This page does not constitute diagnosis, repair, or field work instructions.
Shifts and working hours

The work context shows that 52% work more than 40 hours per week, 52% face time pressure every day, 56% need to make decisions every day, 42% have a lot of decision freedom, 76% need face-to-face discussions every day, and 44% spend most of their time in contact with others; common arrangements include peak-season and appointment scheduling and overtime. When comparing jobs, put the working-hours structure and the overtime and commission or piece-rate arrangements into the written terms.
Continuing training and review

Diagnostic equipment and software, hybrid and electric vehicle high-voltage systems, ADAS and software-defined functions, and refrigerant and emissions regulations update quickly (O*NET lists 16 technology skill categories, of which 9 are hot technologies: Safari 2%, Firefox 2%, Edge 2%, Office 1%, Outlook 1%, Excel 1%, and Word and SAP and Windows each below 1%; the page gives the proportion of appearance based on employer job postings), requiring ongoing continuing training and maintenance of equipment and manuals; before starting, confirm the training arrangements, work authorization, and quality inspection and rework review mechanisms.

paragraphs: Boundary: This section describes occupational risk and boundary management, not an evaluation of an individual or institution; the specific vehicle safety, emissions, high-voltage system, and refrigerant handling requirements, work permits and certifications, and parts sourcing and traceability rules are determined by the applicable jurisdiction, competent authority, and institutional process. This page is based on the official duties, tasks, and work context fields of O*NET 49-3023.00, the U.S. EPA motor vehicle air conditioning (MVAC) Section 609 requirements, OSHA industry hazard material, and the Ministry of Transport of mainland China's Regulations on the Administration of Motor Vehicle Repair.

Direct answer: The main risks include lifting support and under-vehicle work with falls and crushing, exposure to chemicals, refrigerants, and exhaust, hazardous energy from electrical and high-voltage systems and airbags, diagnostic misjudgment and replacing parts instead of diagnosing, loss of control over parts sourcing and the management of replaced and removed parts, and exceeding authorization or unclear work permits; the control approach is to work to applicable standards, first confirm hazardous energy and safety conditions, record truthfully, and accept quality-inspection review.

Evidence scope: The risk and boundary entries are based on the official duties, tasks, and work context fields of O*NET 49-3023.00 (36% consider the consequences of error extremely serious, 46% consider precision or accuracy extremely important, 86% wear common protective or safety equipment every day, 69% are exposed to contaminants every day, 41% are exposed to hazardous equipment every day, 38% are exposed to hazardous conditions every day, 39% are exposed to minor burns, cuts, bites, or stings every day, 83% work indoors in an enclosed vehicle or operate enclosed equipment every day), the U.S. EPA motor vehicle air conditioning (MVAC) Section 609 training and certification requirements, and the common injury events and commonly cited penalty provisions listed in OSHA's Automotive Service and Collision Industry Hazard Information.

The editors suggest checking the lift equipment manual, support points, inspection, and the real stop-work and return-to-work system; Article 23 of the repair regulations requires safety education and compliance, this round obtained no complete lifting procedure for each vehicle model, and work should not be resumed on one's own based on an overview.

It applies only to the corresponding U.S. MVAC scenario, not to a general Chinese auto repair certificate or to licensing for all air conditioning systems. entries.answer: The core is three kinds of tasks: checking key components such as belts and hoses and steering and spark plugs and brake and fuel systems and wheel bearings against a checklist, inspecting vehicle damage and recording findings, reviewing work orders and discussing them with the supervisor, troubleshooting fuel and ignition and emission control system faults with electronic test equipment, road-testing and testing components and systems with diagnostic equipment, and disassembling units and checking wear with micrometers and calipers and gauges; performing routine and scheduled maintenance such as oil changes and lubrication and adjustment, repairing and replacing and adjusting brakes and fuel injectors and filters, repairing and maintaining air conditioning and heating and cooling and electrical systems, overhauling or replacing carburetors and blowers and alternators and distributors and starters and pumps, tuning engines, repairing or replacing pistons and connecting rods and gears and valves and bearings, disassembling and repairing and rebuilding assemblies such as powertrains and steering systems, repairing or rebuilding transmissions, and replacing spark plugs and filters and batteries on hybrid vehicles; communicating symptoms and repair needs with customers and estimating repair costs, testing and adjusting repaired systems to meet manufacturer performance specifications, and keeping the work area clean. On the U.S. side this corresponds to O*NET 49-3023.00, with the official duty of diagnosing, adjusting, repairing, or overhauling motor vehicles.
entries.question: What do automotive service technicians and mechanics do every day?

entries.answer: Mainly lifting and support and under-vehicle work with falls and crushing, exposure to chemicals and refrigerants and exhaust, hazardous energy from electrical and high-voltage systems and airbags, diagnostic misjudgment and replacing parts instead of diagnosing, loss of control over parts sourcing and the management of replaced and removed parts, and exceeding authorization and unclear work permits. The control approach is to work to applicable standards, first confirm hazardous energy and safety conditions, record truthfully, and accept quality-inspection review. This page does not provide diagnosis, repair, or on-site work instructions.
entries.question: What risks should I pay attention to in advance with this job?

entries.answer: The more explanatory signals are: being able to complete inspection and repair and testing to specification and record them truthfully, being able to reason through the cause of a fault following a diagnostic process and judge measured values against manufacturer specifications, and being able to judge safety conditions and authorization boundaries and stop and escalate on anomalies or when work exceeds authorization; 'liking cars' or 'being able to drive' alone cannot determine this. The Holland interest code is RCI (Realistic + Investigative + Conventional), and interest consistency only indicates that the direction is close.
entries.question: How do I judge whether I am suited to being an automotive service technician and mechanic?

entries.answer: AI and automation can change steps such as reading fault codes and retrieving manuals and cases, recording measurements and comparing parameters, and work orders and inventory and estimating and settlement text; but there is no official evidence that it will wholly replace fault-cause judgment, confirming disassembly safety, judging component wear, test and adjustment results, and the conclusions of work involving safety parts and high-voltage systems and refrigerants. Official material also does not give the automation replacement rate or the year the occupation disappears.
entries.question: Which tasks will AI change?

entries.answer: Fault cause and scope judgment, hazardous-energy isolation and verification, confirming disassembly safety, judging component wear, testing and adjusting to manufacturer specifications, and work decisions involving safety parts and high-voltage systems and airbags and refrigerant handling must all be undertaken by the person and by authorized personnel according to institutional procedures; system output must first be marked as reference and may enter the formal work order only after actual-measurement and procedure confirmation and human review.
